questions.question: What is an event in a sample space $S$?
options: A subset $A\subseteq S$ whose occurrence can be assigned a probability
A single number between zero and one
The complete list of all possible outcomes
A rule that chooses the sample space after the experiment
questions.explanation: An event is a subset $A\subseteq S$ of the sample space — a collection of outcomes to which the model can assign a probability.
questions.source_support: The definition says an event is a subset $A\subseteq S$ whose occurrence can be assigned a probability.
option_explanations: A number in $[0,1]$ is a probability VALUE, not an event; events are sets of outcomes.
The complete list of all outcomes is the sample space $S$ itself (the certain event), not a general event.
The sample space is fixed before the experiment; an event does not 'choose' $S$ afterward.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: When does an event $A$ occur?
options: When $\omega$ is outside the sample space
When the realized outcome $\omega$ belongs to $A$
questions.explanation: An event $A$ occurs precisely when the realized outcome $\omega$ is a member of $A$, i.e. $\omega\in A$.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says an event happens exactly when the realized outcome belongs to the event.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: By definition the outcome $\omega$ always lies in $S$; being outside $S$ cannot happen.
An event with no outcomes is $\varnothing$, the impossible event, which never occurs.
No subset of $S$ can be larger than $S$, so this cannot describe occurrence.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For one die roll with $S=\{1,\ldots,6\}$ and $A=\{2,4,6\}$ ('even'), what is the complement event $A^c$?
questions.explanation: The complement of 'even' $=\{2,4,6\}$ is everything in $S$ that is not even, namely the odd rolls $\{1,3,5\}$.
questions.source_support: An event is a subset of $S$; its complement is the rest of $S$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: $\{2,4,6\}$ is the event $A$ itself, not its complement.
$\varnothing$ is the complement of $S$, not of a proper subset.
$S$ is the complement only of the empty event $\varnothing$.

questions.question: Which operations can be used to combine events?
options: Only addition and multiplication of numbers
questions.explanation: Events are sets, so they combine by set operations: union ($A\cup B$), intersection ($A\cap B$) and complement ($A^c$).
questions.source_support: The key results say events can be combined using union, intersection, and complement.
option_explanations: Events are sets of outcomes; arithmetic on numbers does not combine them.
Differentiation and integration act on functions, not on events.
Ordering outcomes alphabetically does not produce a new event.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: What does a probability function assign probabilities to?
options: Only the name of the experiment
questions.explanation: A probability function assigns probabilities to events — the subsets of $S$ in the model.
questions.source_support: A key result states that a probability function assigns probabilities to events, not to informal statements outside the model.
option_explanations: Probabilities attach to events inside the model, not to informal statements outside it.
The name of an experiment is not a set of outcomes, so it gets no probability.
A single largest outcome is not what $P$ is defined on; $P$ acts on events.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For one die roll with $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, which set represents 'roll an even number'?
questions.explanation: 'Even' on a die is the set of even faces $\{2,4,6\}$.
questions.source_support: The examples say the event 'roll an even number' is the set of outcomes two, four, and six.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $\{1,3,5\}$ is the odd numbers — the complement of 'even'.
$\{6\}$ is only one even face; $2$ and $4$ are even too.
$\{1,\dots,6\}$ is all of $S$ (the certain event), not 'even'.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: If $S=\{H,T\}$ for one coin toss, which set is the event 'heads occurs'?
questions.explanation: An event is a SET of outcomes, so 'heads occurs' is the singleton $\{H\}$.
questions.source_support: An event is a subset of the sample space.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $H$ is an outcome (an element), whereas an event must be a set, $\{H\}$.
$\{T\}$ is the event 'tails', the complement of heads.
$\{H,T,H\}$ repeats $H$ and includes $T$; 'heads' is just $\{H\}$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: If $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, which option is not an event in this model?
questions.explanation: Events are subsets of $S=\{1,\dots,6\}$. Since $7\notin S$, $\{7\}$ is not a subset of $S$ and so is not an event here.
questions.source_support: Events are subsets of the sample space.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $\{1,2\}\subseteq S$, so it is a valid event.
$\varnothing$ is the impossible event, a valid subset of $S$.
$S$ is the certain event, a valid subset of itself.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For a survey sample space, the statement 'respondent is under thirty' should be modeled as what?
options: The subset of outcomes whose respondent age is under thirty
A new sample space unrelated to the survey outcomes
One fixed outcome for every respondent
A probability before the relevant outcomes are identified
questions.explanation: 'Respondent is under thirty' is the set of outcomes whose recorded age is below $30$ — a subset of the survey's sample space.
questions.source_support: The examples say that 'respondent is under thirty' collects all outcomes with that property.
option_explanations: An event is a subset of the SAME sample space, not a new unrelated one.
It is a set of many outcomes, not one fixed outcome per respondent.
It is the set itself; the probability is computed afterward, not before.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For events $A$ and $B$, what does $A\cap B$ represent?
options: The event that both $A$ and $B$ occur
The event that either one occurs
questions.explanation: $A\cap B$ is the event that BOTH $A$ and $B$ occur (the outcomes common to both).
questions.source_support: Events are sets, combined with set operations.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: 'Either one occurs' is the union $A\cup B$.
'Neither occurs' is $(A\cup B)^c$.
'The complement of $A$' is $A^c$.

questions.question: Why is an event best treated as a set of outcomes rather than just a sentence?
options: Every event must contain exactly one outcome
Probabilities are assigned only to words, not sets
Set notation makes occurrence and probability assignment precise
questions.explanation: Writing an event as a set of outcomes makes 'the event occurred' ($\omega\in A$) and its probability precise, unlike a vague sentence.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says an event is a statement about the outcome and happens when the realized outcome belongs to it.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Sentences can mention outcomes; the point is precision, not impossibility.
Events may contain many outcomes or none, not exactly one.
Probabilities attach to sets — which is exactly why the set description is used.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For events $A$ and $B$, what does $A\cup B$ represent?
options: The event that $A$ or $B$ (or both) occurs
questions.explanation: $A\cup B$ is the event that $A$ or $B$ (or both) occurs.
questions.source_support: Events combine by union, intersection, and complement.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: 'Both occur' is the intersection $A\cap B$.
'Neither occurs' is $(A\cup B)^c$.
A union is an event (a set), not a single probability value.

questions.question: Why must an event be tied to the chosen sample space?
options: Otherwise its outcomes may not be well-defined inside the model
Because every event has to contain every outcome
Because events are not allowed to be combined
Because probability functions assign values only to sample spaces, not events
questions.explanation: An event must be a subset of the chosen $S$; otherwise its outcomes may not be defined within the model.
questions.source_support: A probability function assigns probabilities to events, not to informal statements outside the model.
option_explanations: Only $S$ contains every outcome; a general event need not.
Events can be combined freely via set operations.
Probability functions assign values to events, not only to $S$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $A=\{1,3,5\}$. If $\omega=3$, what is true?
questions.explanation: $A=\{1,3,5\}$ and $\omega=3\in A$, so the event $A$ occurs.
questions.source_support: An event happens exactly when the realized outcome belongs to the event.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $3\in A$, so $A$ does occur.
$\{1,3,5\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,6\}$, so $A$ is a subset of $S$.
$\omega=3$ is an outcome, not a probability function.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Let $S=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}$. Which event represents 'exactly one head'?
questions.explanation: 'Exactly one head' among $\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}$ is $\{HT,TH\}$.
questions.source_support: Events are collections of outcomes satisfying the stated condition.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $\{HH\}$ is two heads, not exactly one.
$\{TT\}$ is zero heads.
$\{HH,HT,TH\}$ is 'at least one head', which includes the two-head outcome.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which event represents the 'impossible event' in a sample space $S$?
questions.explanation: The impossible event is the empty set $\varnothing$: it contains no outcomes, so it never occurs.
questions.source_support: $S$ is the certain event; $\varnothing$ is the impossible event.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: $S$ is the certain event, which always occurs.
A single outcome can occur, so a singleton is not impossible.
A complement $A^c$ is not generally impossible.

questions.question: Which event is always available once a sample space $S$ is chosen?
options: $A$ with $A$ not contained in $S$, which is not a subset of $S$.
questions.explanation: Once $S$ is chosen, $S$ itself is always an event — the certain event, which always occurs.
questions.source_support: An event is a subset of the sample space.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $S\cup\{x\}$ with $x\notin S$ leaves the sample space, so it is not an event of $S$.
$P(S)$ is a number, not an event or an outcome.
An $A$ not contained in $S$ is not a subset of $S$, hence not an event.
questions.rewrite_notes: stem-option-quality auto-fix: replace generic intensifier on formula/value distractor with substantive misconception tag.

questions.question: Why is $\emptyset$ an event in the usual set-based description?
options: It is a subset of every sample space $S$
It is the same as every single outcome
It has to occur in every experiment
questions.explanation: $\varnothing$ is a subset of every set, so it is always an event in the set-based description.
questions.source_support: Events are subsets of the sample space, and set operations include the empty subset.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Containing all outcomes describes $S$, not $\varnothing$.
$\varnothing$ has no outcomes, so it is not the same as a single outcome.
$\varnothing$ is the impossible event; it never occurs.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Suppose $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $A$ is 'roll at least five'. Which subset is $A$?
questions.explanation: 'Roll at least five' means $X\ge5$, i.e. the faces $\{5,6\}$.
questions.source_support: An event collects all outcomes in the sample space satisfying the stated condition.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is 'less than five', the complement.
$\{4,5\}$ wrongly includes $4$ ($<5$) and omits $6$.
$\{6\}$ omits $5$, which also satisfies $\ge5$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Let $S=[0,+\infty)$ and let $A$ be 'the waiting time is strictly less than 3'. Which event matches $A$?
questions.explanation: 'Waiting time strictly less than $3$' on $S=[0,+\infty)$ is the interval $[0,3)$.
questions.source_support: Events are subsets of the sample space, and waiting-time sample spaces can be all nonnegative times.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $(3,+\infty)$ is times greater than $3$, the opposite.
$\{-3,3\}$ includes a negative time (not in $S$) and is not the set of times $<3$.
$[3,+\infty)$ is times $\ge3$, the complement of $<3$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
